title: The law's bodily works are dead; baptism clothes all with Christ
english: The word is addressed to Peter: you destroyed them by a decree which had been sent from you to Antioch and to the whole world. It is unseemly, then, to teach others what you abandoned and destroyed by your own decree.

The law has its work and its enjoyment in bodily things: eat this, do not eat that, keep the Sabbath, circumcision. Grace does not want you to win approval through these things. So I was made dead to these things, he says. What need do I have of the law? I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. The life I lived for myself—that was under the law. But since Christ lives in me—who is no longer under the law but in heaven at the right hand of the Father—I do not reject the one living in me. And what I now live in the flesh, I live in faith. For I believe in the Son of God. And if the Son of God in whom I believe is at the right hand of the Father, I have my citizenship in heaven; but the law had its observances among things on earth. Therefore I am not subject to the law.

The law weighed more heavily, and for this reason it was named a ministry of death. How then was it added because of transgressions, he says? In a brief word, it is this: before the law, the mind of human beings along with the flesh was enslaved to sin and loved evil; when the law was given, the mind was trained, but the flesh was still held down. Since, then, the one who does not know that sin is sin pursues impiety as piety and attends to it more eagerly, while the one who knows that it is evil gains at least this: the awareness that he is transgressing, and he desires to obey God. This is why the law was given. "A law able to give life" stands for this: if a law was given, it was not given, he says, against the promises of God; but neither could it prevail for all time.
Even if the law accomplished nothing else, it provided the knowledge of God. And the knowledge of God made one ready to receive grace.

It is not the observance of the law, he says, that makes the Jews who believe better than those from the nations, but the power of baptism, which provides the putting on of Christ, makes grace common to all together—barbarians, Greeks, Jews, female, male. He did not add female and male idly (for the point at hand called for only one pair in the statement, Greek and Jew), but to argue that if baptism brings male and female, though different, into one grace, how much more Greek and Jew. [Translator note: ὅσον γὰρ εἷς τῷ ῥήματι ἐζήτει is textually uncertain; rendered by sense.], though different, into one grace, how much more Greek and Jew.

Now he wants to show that after grace has come, even if someone seems to keep the Sabbath according to the law, and new moons and festivals, he is as one committing idolatry to the basic principles he worshiped when he was a Gentile, serving them in another way.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Fragmenta in Epistolam ad Galatas u01-rem-early
orientation: Eusebius is commenting on Paul's words to Peter at Antioch and then on Galatians 2:18–4:10, explaining why the law's bodily observances are dead for the believer and why baptism makes grace common to all.

title: The law has ceased; Paul's allegory is prophecy through deeds
english: And he is not keeping the law, for it has ceased. When he called the basic principles poor, he did not accuse them as evil, but as unable to enrich and to suffice for piety. Paul says, "Do not suppose that I had some other grievance against you and for that reason I rebuke you." The depth of his anguish constantly forces him to change the form of his speech—now rebuking, now encouraging, now accusing, now lamenting. Here, then, he teaches that what he writes, he writes out of affection—for I have been wronged in nothing by you, he says—but also as care, because I have been counted worthy of the very greatest care. What then is the blessedness? That is, there is none. Or rather: is it keeping the law or living by faith? And since he said that the circumcision party do not want to emulate you, so that they themselves may have the perfection of faith without keeping the law, but want you to emulate them, he added: "I say these things not envying them." For would that they also were perfect, having made use of faith, and nothing hindered them from emulating and imitating us. So you also do such things as make you worthy of emulation, so that all may imitate you—and not only when I come, being ashamed before me, do you become such, but even when I am absent, set yourselves right. Now he used the name, not the power, of allegory. For allegory does not follow the literal words, but introduces other things made manifest from the sequence of thoughts according to their texture—such as: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth (Song of Songs 1:2). For there it is neither a kiss, nor hair, nor belly, nor thighs, nor anything else, but other things are introduced through other things, and this is the proper form of allegory. Here, however, the history is acknowledged, and it has been demonstrated that it is a type of what is to come. So the prophecy through deeds has now been named allegory. For of prophecies, some are through words alone, such as: Behold, the virgin shall conceive (Isaiah 7:14); some through deeds alone, as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness (Numbers 21:9); and some through both deeds and words, such as what was said to Jeremiah: Take a new waistcloth and put it on; then bury it by the Euphrates (Jeremiah 13:1–11). And when it had rotted with time and was eaten away, take it from there, he says. For up to this point the prophecy is through deeds, but what follows is also through words: that in this way I also put on the sons of Israel, and in this way I helped them, and in this way I led them captive to Babylon, and when they have rotted and been corrupted there, I bring them up from there and restore them.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Fragmenta in Epistolam ad Galatas u01-rem-mid
orientation: Eusebius is commenting on Galatians 4, explaining that the law has ceased after grace, that Paul's rebukes come from love, and that what Paul calls allegory is really prophecy enacted through historical events.

title: Allegory as enacted prophecy; why Paul mentions sin with the law; sowing to the flesh; only the new creation matters
english: So now he called the prophecy enacted through deeds an allegory. He did not mention Mount Sinai without reason, but because the Hagarenes, the descendants of Ishmael, hold the desert that stretches as far as Mount Sinai. On Sinai the law was given, and it gives birth into slavery. From Mount Sinai the tablets were given and carried into Israel, and after being moved many times from place to place they were finally established in Jerusalem. For this reason he added: she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, and she is in slavery with her children (Galatians 4:25). Where there is an earthly promise, and property, and marriage, and human affairs, slavery follows as well. But where there is release from earthly cares and from bonds, and citizenship is in heaven, freedom comes from that very citizenship.

The question is raised why, in drawing them away from the law, he mentions sin. It is because the law commanded feasting, and through this desire is provoked, and since it is uncontrollable it leads to sin. For this reason, whenever the law is mentioned, he also mentions sin. Indeed, in the letter to the Romans, when he mentions the law he also brings in the correction through the Lord: those who live according to the flesh cannot please God (Romans 8:8). But why was feasting and eating permitted? Because progress in abstaining from acknowledged evils would not have occurred unless eating and drinking had been permitted to them. For the lawgiver knew that it is impossible for those who feast to master their pleasures. For the time being, however, he wanted to train the mind, so that it might know what is good and what is evil and what is godly. For the lawgiver foresaw that Christ was going to come, who would supply what was lacking in the law—I mean not walking according to the flesh, as Paul says.

He made clear from this that many were spending unwisely, giving to those who urged them to keep the law, but giving nothing to those who proclaimed Paul's teaching. Therefore he says: the one who sows to his own flesh. For the person subject to the law lives in fleshly things. Thus the one who gives to the one who teaches these things sows only into the flesh.

So that Paul might not be thought to be advocating uncircumcision and not circumcision, and so that he might not give a pretext for slander to his opponents, he added the final point most beautifully: neither circumcision has any power nor uncircumcision, but he said new creation. About this he says elsewhere (2 Corinthians 5:17): if anyone is in Christ, new creation. If it is a new creation, he says, do not come under the law. For the one living according to the law lives in the world, but the one living in Christ has citizenship in heaven. So the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world (Galatians 6:14).

orientation: Eusebius is closing his commentary on Galatians, explaining Paul's final remarks about Sinai, the law and sin, sowing to the flesh, and the new creation.
